doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Gil's leadership style, taped gigs, and the Paris drummer story
summary: Gil never told anyone what to play or called tunes, taped every gig, drew Mick Jagger to Sweet Basil's; in Paris he told a nervous substitute drummer to quit playing what he thought Gil wanted.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Did people in the band ever go “what is he doing?” Well I mean you just basically said it, talking about the sax players, but did you ever say like oh my God, now he’s got this guy in here.

Well Gil was an institution, I mean before I met him. He led the band, his concept was he wants to see where the music can go. That is the whole thing, that sums it up. Some nights the band was pretty loose and some nights it was great. If we had a bad night everybody knew it, it happened. When the band was really on, the impact was incredible. It could happen for a lot of reasons, but sometimes just playing the arrangements themselves sometimes a couple of guys in the band would really be up and would have a great night and would catch an audience at the right time and it was like being at a pop concert as far as audience reaction was concerned, which obviously is not the bottom line criteria for doing jazz. But the band had a tremendous impact and Gil did very little to actually direct it. He never told anybody what to do, what to play. If he didn’t like the way you played you just wouldn’t be there, you’d get fired or laid off or something. And he very seldom — it didn’t happen very often, he wouldn’t even explain why he was doing it — he would just well, “I’ve got to change this,” and it would change. But he never told anybody what to play. Well once — great story — I’ve got time to do this before I forget. He didn’t call the tunes. He would just sit at the piano and just kind of wait between tunes and then he would just start playing something and would leave it to us to figure out what tune it was he was playing. And we would eventually all find it and the rhythm section would find it and get something going. And then he might or might not give us just a cue, okay, start playing the chart. More often than not we’d get into the groove of the chart and somebody would stand up and solo and there’d be a couple of solos and then maybe then we’d play the chart. And this could go on for a set that started at 11:30 at night at Sweet Basil’s and end at two in the morning, and Gil would stand up and look around and say, “Did we play an hour yet?” And that’s it. That’s the way the band was. It was wonderful. But the key was having Gil there. Because of who he was he was so universally respected, I don’t know if I could describe what a tangible that thing was at the time, but you couldn’t — there’s just no way you could be on his bandstand and play something jive. Because he made a cassette of everything. Every gig he ever

played. If you played something jive you’d hear about it the next week. “Don’t do that anymore. Don’t do that.” But it was typical. We’d be playing some late night set at Sweet Basil’s on a Monday night and someone like Mick Jagger would be sitting in a dark corner with glasses on trying to be as inconspicuous as possible, just kind of listening to the band. Wow. And just a bunch of New York guys playing jazz and taking far too long solos and a leader that didn’t want to lead. But it was just the respect, it was unspoken but it was felt for Gil, it was an incredible thing, largely because of what he had done in the past, but also he led the Gil Evans Orchestra in that stage and then went on to the 70s and most of the 80s. So it wasn’t all based on “Sketches of Spain” and like a couple of good charts and a hit record. It was a lot more than that. I’ll be quick. The one story that I was thinking of, we were somewhere in Europe, we were in Paris. And I can’t remember why but we had lost the drummer. The drummer had to go home. So we came into Paris, we were playing at a club, it was a big club, it was in a basement, I think it used to be a subway station or something, I don’t remember the name of it, it was a long time ago. Although we came into town and we had no drummer. Steve Lacy I think played the concert. I don’t know if he was on the tour or not but Steve lived in Paris. So he’s got a young drummer that he’s using in his own band and why don’t we use this guy. He said fine, sounds good. It was a young guy, good player. He was really nervous. I mean he was just totally intimidated by the situation, which can happen. The club was kind of this basement thing, it was all stone with archways over our head. There was no seating, everybody was just seated on the floor all around us. So we were in the bandstand, like there were people right up to the edge of us sitting cross-legged. And we played a few tunes and Gil typically wouldn’t call the tunes between, he would just sit at the piano and think for a while or he’d stand up and rock back and forth and sit down and start playing something. So we were in one of those minute gaps between tunes, like what’s going to happen. And Gil walked over to this young drummer, who had been trying so hard, trying to read the book, and it just wasn’t working. And we all kind of knew that it wasn’t that he couldn’t play, he could play, but it just was not working. Gil just walked over to him and looked him in the face and said, “Quit playing what you think I want you to play.” That’s it. And he grabbed the book. Took the drum book, walked back to the piano, and he called “Gone” the uptempo of the thing from “Porgy & Bess,” which is a big drum feature. And it’s all asymmetrical. It’s not like the band plays eight bars, the drummer plays eight bars, nothing like that. It’s totally asymmetrical. There’s no way you could play it without the chart. But it’s like okay we’re going to play, we’re leaving space for the drums, do what you do. Just do it. It didn’t work but it was — he tried. But that line, “Quit playing what you think I want you to play,” that could have applied to any one of us. I was lucky he never said it to me.
Anyway that was Gil. How long did I spend answering that question? I’m sorry.
